blocks.html: Eduarda stayed all morning and all afternoon, without getting up from the armchair until eight that evening. She stayed without lunch, without a snack, without dinner, forgetting she still had basic needs, like going to the bathroom. She stayed when they took Lorena away for tests and brought her back. She stayed until the day was over. She stayed without anyone insisting that she leave or get out of the ICU. Not Gerluce, not Paulo, not Henrique even bothered to try.

The thought of Lorena waking up alone in that place, still frightened after an extubation that would remain traumatic in her memory for a long time, was unthinkable to her. So Eduarda wasn't leaving. She wouldn't move, wouldn't sleep, wouldn't give up her seat.

Every time Lorena woke, Eduarda's face would be the first thing she saw. Every time Lorena fell asleep, it would be the last. At least she could fight off the lingering effects of the sedatives in peace, certain that Eduarda would always be there, caring for her, looking after her, watching over her as she slept, stroking the arch of her eyebrow and her hands.
Anyone who tried to argue that she didn't have to take being there quite so literally would lose that argument to the evidence coming from the heart monitor's beeps.

As the day passed in cycles, Lorena would wake with a start, her heart rate spiking and the alarms going off whenever she remembered what was happening. Her eyes would slowly open, find Eduarda and her reassuring smile, and everything would settle down again.
It was concrete, scientific, irrefutable proof. Eduarda Fragoso was still her best medicine.

Eduarda stayed when Maggye and Leonardo were the first to come in, so emotionally paralyzed they couldn't bring themselves to sit down. They remained standing beside the bed, studying Lorena, unsure what to say while she slept. Leonardo chose silence, looking at his sister with one hand against his face at the level of his mask and pain in the eyes visible above the fabric. Somehow, he could feel her pain. He always had.

Ever since they broke half the plates in one of Zenilda’s Portuguese dinnerware sets while playing ball inside the house, and discovered what it meant to be partners in crime when they tried to cover up their first childhood misdeed together. Ever since he tried to teach her to ride a bicycle without their parents knowing, and Lorena fell, knocked out a baby tooth—the permanent one later grew in crooked—and cried for hours at the amount of blood pouring from her mouth. Ever since some idiot boy at their school asked her out in sixth grade and, after she turned him down, turned half the class against her with lies and bullying that went on for months, until Leonardo cornered him in the bathroom. Ever since she returned from Italy and they had that conversation in their mother’s living room, when she told him about her diagnosis for the first time.

He didn’t need to say anything for Eduarda to understand. It was written all over his face. As much as she, Maggye, and Paulo had been part of all this for years, just as there was a world that belonged to the two of them alone, there was a world that belonged only to the Ferette siblings, and Leonardo was afraid of losing that, too. He didn’t know how to be without Lorena. He didn’t know how to exist without being her older brother. It had been that way since the first time he held her in his arms, clumsy because he was still so small himself, but determined to be brave and show that he was already a man.

Maggye bent down, whispered a few loving words that Lorena couldn’t hear, and stroked her head for long minutes before leaving. She, too, carried a grief of her own, one that, like everyone else’s, was singular and impossible to share with anyone.
The grief of having witnessed the lowest points in Lorena’s life. Of having opened the test results that revealed the diagnosis beside her, never imagining that one day they would reach this point.

Maggye might not share the blood bond between Leonardo and Lorena, but she knew that, in the end, it made no difference. Her life had revolved around Custode for years and, consequently, around Lorena. They had become a family, filling the empty spaces in each other in different ways. For Lorena, it was the pain of being forced apart. For Maggye, it was the emotional distance from her own family. In her own way, she didn’t know how to be without Lorena, either.

Paulinho and Gerluce came in together a little later. Unlike Leonardo, Paulo sat beside Eduarda, took her hand in his left and Lorena’s in his right, and stayed there for a while, wishing he could lift the weight of the whole world off his two girls. For long minutes, tears slipped from his red, irritated eyes and disappeared behind his mask. Paulo had always been like that, from beginning to end. A terrible actor who would lose everything if his life depended on concealing his feelings. It was his touch, in fact, that woke Lorena.

Her eyes opened slowly, heavy with sleep as she felt someone caressing her hand. She looked at Eduarda, at Paulinho, at Gerluce, who was there more to support them than because she felt entitled to be. Lorena tried to lift her head, only to grow frustrated when she realized that the few hours that had passed still weren’t enough to let her make a movement that had once been so simple. She tried to speak, only to discover that she would need more time before she could escape the mental prison of having so much to say and being unable to say any of it.

Violeta and Henrique decided not to go in. With Lorena waking and growing more alert, Henrique didn’t want to put her through the stress of seeing someone again whom she had spent years believing would hate her more than anyone for everything he had done to Eduarda. He would have time to catch up with Lorena, and this was nowhere near the right moment.

In the end, only one person was missing. If each of them carried a particular kind of pain, just as Lorena held a particular place in each of their lives, Zenilda’s pain was impossible to share. Of them all, she alone was afraid of losing a daughter.

Eduarda had barely lingered on any of the others, glancing toward the door when they entered and exchanging a quick, acknowledging smile before turning her attention back to Lorena. But when Zenilda came in, their eyes met for what felt like an eternity.
They were reflections of each other in a mirror. Two sides of the same coin.

Zenilda saw herself every day in Eduarda’s anguished expressions. Eduarda saw herself every day in Zenilda’s eyes, now permanently swollen and red. If Leonardo and Maggye didn’t know how to be without Lorena, if Paulinho felt impossibly small each time he entered that room, Zenilda and Eduarda were wasting away alongside her, day after day, as the illness took its toll.

She entered slowly, pushing the door open with care, almost dragging herself forward, as though her strength were failing her, too. She stopped, took a deep breath, studied Lorena in the bed, and closed her eyes in relief at seeing her without the tube. Cristina had already confirmed that everything had gone well. Even so, Zenilda needed to see it for herself. It was a mother’s need.
Eduarda watched her approach without a word. Zenilda’s steps carried her to the empty chair beside Eduarda, the same one Paulo had occupied near the head of the bed.
Zenilda sat down and let her entire attention settle on Lorena.

She was sleeping peacefully. Apart from her clearly weakened body and the changes in her appearance, it could have been an ordinary sleep. Eduarda kept quiet, giving Zenilda the space and time she needed to look at her. It was an easy feeling to understand. Whenever Eduarda was there, she had little attention left for anyone or anything other than Lorena in front of her.

Zenilda leaned forward slowly and took Lorena’s hand with care, afraid of waking her. She brought Lorena’s fingers to her face and pressed them against the cheek hidden beneath her mask, as though she needed to feel her touch. Then she lowered her daughter’s arm back onto the mattress, stroking it while a few tears slipped silently down her cheeks.

Eduarda watched without speaking, seeing in Zenilda’s eyes how far away her thoughts had gone. She wasn’t seeing the thirty-three-year-old Lorena lying in that bed. She was seeing the newborn baby, still covered in blood, whom she had held while the child was still crying after an exhausting labor. The little girl who used to run through the house with Leonardo. The withdrawn teenager she had been until the day she met Eduarda. Every stage of her life folded into one. Until she had been forced to live in another country and no longer rely on her mother’s protection—precisely when, without Zenilda knowing it, she had needed her arms more than ever.

She gently stroked Lorena’s forehead, missing the dark strands of hair she had loved running her fingers through as she caressed her head. Maybe one day she could make up for all the nights Lorena had spent alone, all the moments when she had longed for that kind of care and hadn’t had it. Maybe one day she could make up for all the lost time.

“Is everything okay? Cristina said the extubation went smoothly,” Zenilda said after a few minutes, her hand still outstretched toward the bed. Her fingers moved along Lorena’s arm as though she needed to touch her to make sure no one would dare take her away.

“Everything is under control, as much as it can be. Extubation is a delicate process. It’s not exactly pleasant, but she did well,” Eduarda said with a half-smile, revealing a pride she wished she didn’t feel.
Lorena was an excellent patient. Cooperative, calm, and, most of the time, she barely complained. It wasn't the kind of thing Eduarda would ever have wanted to find out.

“She’s very weak and can’t speak yet, but that’s normal. Her body and throat will need time to recover,” she explained, once again tracing the line of Lorena’s eyebrow while Zenilda occupied herself with the space between Lorena’s wrist and elbow.

“More physical therapy?” Zenilda asked, frustration in her voice, and Eduarda nodded, understanding her point. It was an exhausting cycle. Every time Lorena recovered from one thing, something else came up. Every time they took ten steps forward, Lorena slipped backward again, right back to square one. Her only fear was that once Lorena could think clearly, she would reach the same conclusion and lose hope.
“There's not much we can do.” She gave a vague answer, because neither of them had a choice.
The only way out of that hospital was to face yet another course of recovery. Probably the hardest one of all, but Eduarda wasn't going to get into that now.
“And you? How are you? How have you been processing all of this?” Zenilda rested her free hand on Eduarda’s shoulder, and Eduarda was startled by the gentle touch against the side of her neck.
Zenilda cared. There was no question about that. But she shouldn't be worrying about Eduarda right now. It was hard to understand how Zenilda still had room to hold anything other than Lorena.

“I... don’t know,” Eduarda hesitated, realizing she hadn’t stopped to think about how she felt. “I think I’m a little relieved, but not enough to feel at ease. Extubation is always difficult to watch, but I was... happy...” She grimaced. “Happy definitely isn’t the right word, but anyway. I’d take this a thousand times over. Being here with her instead of waiting outside. That’s what I miss most about when I was still on the team. Being able to be there for moments like this. It helps both of us.”

Zenilda smiled faintly, wondering when Eduarda had become this woman. Devoted down to the last strand of her hair. Strong. Mature. Fearless. Because she couldn't find any other word for the way Eduarda set aside every fear and feeling of her own just to be there whenever Lorena needed her.

“I don’t know how to thank you. For everything,” Zenilda said, looking away from Lorena for a few seconds to meet Eduarda’s eyes. “You’ve been our rock, Duda. I honestly don’t know if Lorena would be holding up without you here. Or if any of us would.”
Eduarda lowered her head as Zenilda's hand rested on her shoulder, moved up her neck, and stroked her ear with her fingertips. The gesture made her throat tighten.

She knew she was piling up emotions and dealing with the weight of them using whatever crutches she could find. Violeta's coffee. Sleeping pills. The tears that escaped despite her efforts. Throwing herself into studying the code of ethics so she could defend herself. The nights at the hospital.

Eduarda was trying with every ounce of strength she had not to fall apart, but controlling herself was difficult when Zenilda treated her this way. Still, she held on. She was afraid she wouldn't be able to get back on her feet once everything came crashing down. Lorena still needed her standing.

“I’m telling you this because I truly am grateful. Because I want you to know how important you are to this family. But you don’t have to carry everything on your shoulders alone, Dudinha. We’re worried about you. All of us.” Hearing the nickname was what finally undid her.

Eduarda let herself lean into Zenilda, resting her head against her shoulder in search of comfort. She felt Zenilda shift, felt the kiss pressed through the mask against the side of her face, and stayed there. Letting herself be held as she wiped away the tears that fell and watched Lorena.

She never answered Zenilda's remark, because she didn't know what to say. She understood that she wasn't obligated to carry the world on her shoulders. She understood the worry that had made Paulo pick up the phone, brought her father from another state, and made Zenilda hold her cheek and Lorena's hand at the same time. But even so, Eduarda felt she had no choice.

In the end, she didn't need to answer. Before she could find the words, Lorena stirred, setting off a chain reaction. Zenilda went still, her hand still against Eduarda's face. Eduarda lifted her head slightly—not enough to pull away, just enough to see better.

By the time Lorena blinked, the part of her subconscious that was still working already knew what she would find. But when she managed to focus her blurry, unfixed gaze, she found not only Eduarda but the two people she loved most in the world, side by side, right beside her.

Eduarda resting against Zenilda's shoulder, receiving the tenderness she deserved, the tenderness Lorena wished so badly she could offer her too. Zenilda looking after her Duda the way she would have, if she could.

Her lips moved in what was meant to be a smile, but her dry mouth pulled painfully. Lorena tried to move her tongue to moisten it, but she could barely manage even that. She closed her eyes, exhausted and frustrated, and opened them again when she heard the voice beside her.

“Hi, sweetheart.” Her eyelids lifted as she looked at Zenilda, who wore the same worried expression as always. The same tired face. Her pupils stood out like two lost islands in a sea of red. “We're here. You don't have to worry about anything. Everyone's okay. Everyone's happy you're awake. All you need to do is rest and get better, too.”

Lorena wanted to answer, but she couldn't. Her muscles barely worked well enough for her to swallow her own saliva. Stubbornly, she tried to shift in bed, but even the slightest movement was enough to bring the pain deep in her abdomen flaring back.
“What is it? What do you need?” Eduarda straightened and leaned forward, resting a hand on Lorena's neck when she sensed something was bothering her.

Lorena's lips moved from side to side, and remembering her first stay in the ICU, Eduarda understood. She stood, picked up the clean gauze and the glass of water Cristina had left for exactly this moment. She slowly wet the gauze and brought it to Lorena's mouth, touching it gently to her lips as Lorena grimaced again, trying to reach for more.

“You can't drink water yet, babe. We'll start giving you food and fluids by mouth again little by little.” Eduarda didn't bother explaining that Lorena's throat muscles were still far too weak to swallow. Any attempt could make her choke, even if merely moistening her lips from the outside did little to ease the discomfort.
Even so, Lorena looked at her as though thanking her, watching while Eduarda moistened the gauze once more and repeated the process with all the care and tenderness in the world.

Zenilda watched, stroking Lorena's wrist as she blinked again while Eduarda tended to her mouth and her mother played gently with her hand. It was the first time since extubation that she'd woken without setting off a storm of beeps around the room. As if some part of her mind could sense, even before her eyes opened, the protection radiating from the two people beside her.

As quickly as she'd woken, Lorena fell asleep again. Eduarda kept moistening her lips for a few more seconds, until she was sure sleep would carry the discomfort away. Then she threw out the used gauze and set some more aside in case Lorena woke again.
“I think it's beautiful, you know,” Zenilda said with a smile. “The way you understand her without her having to say a word.” Eduarda smiled back, settling into the armchair.

“That's what years of practice will do.” Zenilda resumed stroking Lorena's arm while Eduarda did the same to the top of her head. Silence stretched between them, and they stayed there, taking care of what mattered most, each in her own way, with whatever weapons she had left to fight with.

“I will never forgive him,” Zenilda said after a while. “Not just for everything he did to you both, for all the suffering he caused. I will never forgive Santiago for the time he stole from me and my daughter.” Eduarda raised her eyes to Zenilda's, lost and reflecting the same anger that had burned in them during the confrontation with her ex-husband.
She nodded, because she understood perfectly. She'd had the very same thought more than once.

If Lorena's time was running out, five years would be precious beyond measure. Five years that would never come back, that they might never be able to make up for. Five years they would miss every day. If anything happened to Lorena, Eduarda couldn't live with the knowledge that she'd lost all that time because of Santiago's inexplicable choices. He would pay for it. One way or another.
Noticing the hard look that had settled over Eduarda's face, Zenilda took her hand again. It was just one more pain they shared, and perhaps one only the two of them truly understood.
That afternoon, Zenilda stayed too, without eating, sleeping, or moving, torn between caring for Lorena and caring for Eduarda, until they were finally made to leave.

Lorena woke the next day certain she'd lost her most basic sense of time, space, and memory. When she blinked, feeling a little more alert and a little more human for the first time in twenty-four hours, she realized she had no idea what date it was, what time it was, or what had happened since her last memory, which was still muddled and difficult to retrieve.

Little by little, she was discovering just how essential routine was to keeping a life in order. Meals and daylight helped mark the hours. Nights of sleep helped count the days. Days helped count the weeks. And weeks marked the time she had spent there.

But her nourishment was limited to a feeding tube, because her intestines needed complete rest and weren't ready for solid food. The sedatives had thrown her sleep cycle entirely out of balance. Daylight came through the ICU window, which at least helped her tell morning from afternoon and night. Yet when she blinked and instinctively tried to move, her best sense of time came from the slight weight on the edge of the mattress to the right of her body, the warmth of a hand resting over hers, and the pain.

Eduarda was in her usual position. Sitting in the armchair beside the bed, leaning forward with her head resting on the edge of the mattress as she slept. One arm was stretched out to hold Lorena's hand; the other was tucked beneath her neck, attempting to make an improvised pillow in place of the real one abandoned in her lap.

Her presence was enough to tell Lorena that morning had passed and it was already midafternoon, when ICU visiting hours began. She vaguely remembered the previous day's visitors. Paulinho crying. Eduarda leaning against her mother's shoulder. Cristina coming into the room to tell them they would have to leave at eight sharp.

Even more faintly, she remembered the two of them soothing her to sleep before the clock struck the hour, so it would be easier and they wouldn't have to say goodbye. The rest of the night had passed in fragments, between consciousness and oblivion, pain and discomfort, only for her to wake and remember she was alone in that place. A few tests in the morning, and nothing else. A blank stretch in her memory.
Lorena let out a frustrated sigh, realizing she couldn't hold on to the memories, but the movement of her chest as she breathed was enough to remind her of much bigger problems.
Her body protested immediately. Everything hurt in one way or another. The surgical site was by far the worst, but other signs of weakness stretched from head to toe.

The pressure and pain in the center of her chest. Muscles that still weren't properly obeying her commands. Her back and hips, stiff and aching from lying in the same position for far too long. Her mouth so dry that the skin had split and stung in places, and a thirst she could hardly bear.
The only obvious improvement was her throat. Although it still hurt, swallowing saliva was a little less uncomfortable. She tried to speak and, for the first time, felt a faint sound escape.
Her eyes shot downward at once, checking whether she'd woken Eduarda.
Lorena watched her carefully, noticing the plaid Custode blanket wrapped around her knees and slipping down her legs, one corner brushing the floor, almost falling.

It was hard to worry about someone else when she could barely take care of herself, but Lorena wondered whether Eduarda was sleeping properly, whether she was going home, whether she was eating. During visiting hours, every time Lorena woke, she was there. Every time she fell asleep, too. This was the first time she'd found Eduarda asleep, and waking her hardly seemed like a good idea. Still, Lorena slowly tested her limits.

She tried to lift her right hand, trapped beneath Eduarda's palm, managing a slightly wider movement for the first time. Her fingers slipped free, and Eduarda stirred, but not enough to wake. Lorena managed a smile, feeling the cuts in her dry lips sting, but kept going. Her hand came to rest, gentle and weak, on Eduarda's head, covered by one of her colorful little caps, and she softly stroked her ear.

“Duda.” Her voice came out weak, almost unrecognizable. Lorena cleared her throat, feeling it burn as a dry cough caught her. Then she took a deep breath and tried again. “Duda.” This time the sound was firmer.

Eduarda stirred slowly, squeezing her eyes shut and furrowing her brow. She blinked a few times, trying to get her bearings too, struggling to make sense of time and place when her routine, always a little chaotic because of her shifts, now seemed worse than ever.

Several seconds passed before she realized she was at the hospital. Eduarda knew she'd slept badly in the oncology break room because she'd refused to spend that first night at home, away from Lorena. She knew she'd spent the morning waiting for visiting hours, after forcing herself to eat lunch at the rooftop café. She remembered coming in with Zenilda, finding Lorena asleep, leaning against the bed to rest for a moment, and now hearing her name.
Her whole body froze at that last thought. Lorena was calling her name.

Eduarda jolted awake, the way you do in a nightmare when you suddenly fall from a great height. Her head shot up, her heart raced, and the room snapped into focus, with lights that were far too bright and air-conditioning that was far too cold. The blanket finished sliding off her legs and landed on the floor. She frowned at the plaid fabric of Lorena's Custode throw, with no idea how it had gotten there. A tender gesture from Zenilda, who had covered her and left her a pillow to use.
Eduarda rubbed her face, wincing at the ache in her spine from the awkward position, and stared at Lorena, unable to decide whether she was dreaming.

Her eyes were open, tired but more alert than they'd been the last few times. Her mouth moved slightly, a few places threatening to split and bleed from dryness. It was a smile. And confirmation that Eduarda wasn't hallucinating came a moment later.

“Hi, love,” Lorena said, her voice hoarse and weak, yet strong enough to split Eduarda in two. She felt the tears coming before she was even fully awake. Her chin trembled, her eyes stung at the sound of those simple words, words that meant so much.

The touches on her face and neck were too real to be a dream. She looked down and found Lorena's hand reaching toward her, despite the IV line secured near her elbow. Her fingers brushed Eduarda's cheeks, traced beneath her eyes, then moved up to her ear and the back of her neck. Hearing her voice had already been almost too much, but feeling Lorena's affection, knowing how hard she had to struggle just to move, was the final straw.
Eduarda sighed, closing her eyes and letting the tears spill. Never again—never—would she fail to appreciate these small gestures that had once seemed so ordinary.
“Don't cry, Duda. Please. I can't stand seeing you and my mom cry anymore.”

Lorena spoke slowly, one word at a time, leaving long pauses between them, but for the first time she managed an entire sentence. It was the thought that had been circling through her sluggish mind since she'd woken. She hated having become a source of so much suffering.

Eduarda nodded, took a deep breath, and wiped her face, because she knew seeing her cry all the time really wasn't good for Lorena. She tried to pull herself together, looking into the green eyes staring back at her. She'd never known she could be so happy simply to see someone alive.

“I'm sorry, babe. But these are happy tears. I promise. They're not sad tears. I'm just so, so happy I can hear your voice.” Lorena tried to smile again, but her mouth tightened painfully and she closed her eyes. Eduarda noticed, just as she'd noticed her silent request for water earlier, and turned toward the bedside table.

“Come here,” she said, a request that sounded halfway like an order, in that unmistakably Eduarda tone Lorena knew so well. It was hard to understand what she meant by come here, given that Lorena couldn't actually move, but it became clear when Eduarda picked up a paper cup.

“I spoke to Cristina when I got here about your mouth bothering you, and she said you can have ice chips now. But slowly,” she explained, again in that authoritative voice that made Lorena smile. “Your digestive tract is still very weak, and so is your throat. I can only give you a little, but it'll help. Swallow carefully so you don't choke.”
She scooped up a small portion of crushed ice with the spoon, and Lorena watched.
“Yes, ma'am, Dr. Fragoso,” she teased. Eduarda rolled her eyes, unable to keep a huge smile from breaking out when she realized Lorena had recovered some of her humor, too.

Eduarda brought the spoon to her lips and, grimacing at the sting where they had cracked, Lorena managed to swallow a few spoonfuls. After the fifth, she raised her hand to show that was enough. She was still thirsty, still dry-mouthed, but far too tired to keep pushing herself. Eduarda set the cup back on the bedside table, and Lorena sank into the mattress, breathing deeply as exhaustion washed over her from the simple effort of swallowing.
“Better?” She heard the question and opened her eyes to look at Eduarda.
Before Lorena could think, Eduarda was there, one elbow resting on the bed as she ran the tips of her fingers that weren't in the splint along the curve of Lorena's eyebrow.

Lorena wanted to go back to sleep. Eduarda's caresses had always had that drowsy effect on her body. But determined to stay awake for a few hours this time, she forced herself to keep her eyes open and nodded, using the chance to look at Eduarda as motivation not to close them.
“Are you okay?” Lorena asked. Eduarda kept stroking her face. Behind the mask, just inches away, her eyes held an expression Lorena couldn't quite read.

“You're asking me if I'm okay?” Eduarda asked with an ironic smile. “I'm not the one who nearly gave everybody a heart attack, babe. I should be asking you whether you're okay.” Lorena sighed, trying to decide whether to press her or answer.

“I'll tell you if you tell me.” She found a compromise, and Eduarda smiled, fully aware she was being blackmailed. Even so, she gave in, distracting herself for a few seconds with the path her fingers traced above Lorena's left eye, careful not to bump the oxygen cannula still fitted beneath her nose to help with her weakened breathing.

“You scared me,” Eduarda repeated, as she'd already said several times. Lorena nodded to show she understood and decided to return the gesture, raising her hand to stroke Eduarda's face while she spoke. “It hasn't been the easiest week of my life. I was... so... so afraid I'd lose you,” she stammered, on the verge of tears again. “Paulinho ended up calling my dad. I told you about it while you were waking up, but I don't know if you remember.”

Lorena was certain Eduarda was downplaying things, and that she'd keep doing it for a long time, perhaps forever. She was certain Eduarda did the same when she spoke about the past, about what their years apart had been like for her, about her pain.

Sometimes Lorena wondered whether they'd ever be able to talk honestly about these things. Whether Eduarda would ever truly open up. Talk about the feelings wounded by their breakup, the distance, the illness. Lorena knew she kept too much to herself. She swallowed everything in silence, and it seemed less and less fair that Lorena should always be the center of everyone's care.

“I don't know what I remember,” Lorena admitted, sensing that pushing Eduarda to talk wouldn't get her anywhere. “I remember you and my mom talking about the surgery. More than once. I remember us talking in the room about your visit to your dad's house. Asking you to help me to the bathroom, and then...” Her memory stopped there.
She tried over and over to retrieve anything beyond those memories, but she couldn't.
“Was I really unconscious for a whole week?” Eduarda nodded, for the first time showing the exhaustion that was consuming her.

“Six days, if you want to be precise. But yes.” Lorena stared at the wall on the other side of the ICU, trying to process that information. Unlike the light sedation during the pneumonia, this time she remembered nothing. She hadn't heard a thing.
“And have you been taking care of yourself? Eating? Sleeping? Or did you spend the entire time here, arguing with everybody? If Paulo called your dad, things definitely weren't good.”

Eduarda continued playing with Lorena's face as Lorena did the same to hers, a shared tenderness that said so much. They were simple, subtle touches, yet somehow they carried and stood for all the longing they'd felt. That insatiable need to always be together, never again to find out what might pull them apart. Threats. Miles. Time. A marriage cut short. Eduarda hoped she'd never have to add another item to the list of reasons she'd lost Lorena. Especially death.

“I already told you I'm okay, babe. Tired, but okay,” she repeated. Lorena was hardly convinced, with the feeling that Eduarda was losing weight as quickly as her own sick body. Her bones seemed more prominent than before. She was still beautiful, always would be, but Lorena felt as if the expressions on her face were aging years in mere days.

“And are you feeling anything? Pain? Tell me the truth,” Eduarda asked, one question tumbling after another. “Were you feeling something before you passed out in the bathroom and didn't tell me? Do you think you can remember?”
Lorena went still, trying to put her thoughts back in order, unsure where to begin.

“My back hurts like hell. I think it's from lying here,” she said, trying to be honest, her voice still hoarse and tired. “My throat is better, but talking is still a little hard. What's bothering me most, though, is my abdomen and chest. I can't move without getting this horrible pain in my stomach and here.” She placed a hand between her breasts.
Eduarda bit her lip, not knowing what to say. Not knowing how to explain it to Lorena. Whether she should tell her or pretend none of it had happened. But Lorena had a right to know.

“I'll talk to Cristina again about your pain medication dosage, but unfortunately the pain is normal. You're going to have a hard time for a while, babe. Moving around, getting up, sitting down. I know it sucks, but it's part of recovery. I'll be right here with you the whole time. Whatever you need,” Eduarda assured her. Her gaze drifted while she continued stroking Lorena's face, not needing to watch what she was doing to know exactly where her fingers were tracing. Lorena noticed the silence.
Her brows drew together at Eduarda's distant, thoughtful expression.

“I don't want to frighten you or alarm you, but the pain in your chest...” She hesitated, rubbing her face with her free hand before looking at Lorena again. “You went into cardiac arrest during surgery, love. It hurts because they had to perform chest compressions to bring you back. That's why you're sore. That's normal, too. They have to use a lot of force on your chest. But nothing broke, not even a rib. They ran tests as soon as they could to make sure.”

At some point Lorena stopped listening. She was trying to process the words, but the sentences scattered inside her head. Her eyes remained fixed on the stitching of the blanket as Eduarda's voice repeated cardiac massage and chest compressions, down to every detail. The way her voice had weakened as she said it, as though she were losing her nerve. One more subject stacked onto the list of things she kept inside and preferred never to discuss with anyone.

So many things made sense now. The time she'd spent unconscious. The way Eduarda had looked at her since the day before, as if checking that Lorena was really there. Paulinho's call to Henrique. For the first time, Lorena understood just how close she'd come to never coming back.

She looked at Eduarda and tried to put herself in her place. Tried to imagine what she would have done if their roles had been reversed, and the mere thought of losing her that way brought tears to her eyes.

“You need to tell me if you feel anything at all, do you understand?” Eduarda insisted, noticing the thoughtful look on her face. “I don't care how small it is. A headache, a twinge, any change in your body—you have to tell me, Lorena. I can't believe you didn't feel anything before you fainted. Part of your intestine was necrotic! There's no way you didn't feel anything!” Her voice rose slowly, word by word, note by note, just as the tears gathered in the corners of her eyes. Her words tumbled out tangled with her feelings. Everything was piling up at once, and Eduarda was close to exploding.

“Duda. Look at me. Easy,” Lorena whispered. Her body forgot its limitations and instinctively tried to sit up to get closer, but she let out a sharp breath of pain as her abdomen seemed to tear. Eduarda moved, pressing her hands to Lorena's chest in alarm. But Lorena caught her chin to keep her from getting distracted. “Look at me,” she repeated.

“It's okay. I'm okay. I'm here with you.” Eduarda nodded, letting a few tears escape. Lorena swallowed hard as she watched Eduarda's chest heave. For a moment she was afraid Eduarda might become ill, that she'd need to call for help and wouldn't be able to. She was clearly hyperventilating. But just as quickly as the feeling had come, it passed when Eduarda took a deep breath, closed her eyes, and regained control.

“I swear I didn't feel anything. I had a little discomfort, you know, like when you eat something that doesn't agree with you? But I thought it was the chemo, the nausea. I never imagined it could be anything more serious.” Eduarda nodded again, still unable to speak, much less explain how she'd managed to swallow the anxiety attack she refused to have in front of Lorena. “Will you forgive me anyway?” Those words stopped her cold.

“Forgive you for what, babe?” The question caught somewhere between a nervous laugh and a sob; she could no longer tell her own feelings apart. Lorena sighed, wiping her face with her fingertips. Eduarda drew a deep breath and tried to make herself stop crying.

“For making you suffer so much. I feel like your life's been a mess since I came back. All you do is stay at this hospital. You don't do anything else. You spend all your time with me, always worried, nervous, scared...” Eduarda cut her off before she could go on.

“Stop. I'm exactly where I want to be.” Her words were firm. “My life didn't become a mess because you came back. My life became a mess when you left. Those are completely different things.” Lorena listened, unable to shake the feeling that she understood. “If anything in my life makes sense right now, it's having you back. It's the only thing that's made sense in these last five years. But you have to promise me you'll tell me about anything that feels different. Even if you don't think it matters.”
Lorena nodded. It was an easy promise to keep, except for the small detail that she didn't want Eduarda to worry about her all the time. Trying to lighten the mood, she smiled.
“Anything? Like, absolutely anything?” Lorena asked. Eduarda nodded, frowning at the possibility that Lorena was already feeling something and keeping it to herself.

“Because I'm feeling something strange right here.” Lorena pointed to her chest, and Eduarda shifted uneasily, afraid of what was coming. “This tightness, you know? Different from the pain of the compressions. Sometimes it feels like I can't breathe. That's how desperately in love with you I am.”
It took Eduarda a second to understand the joke. She would have smacked Lorena's arm if she hadn't caught herself at the last moment and remembered her condition.
“Fuck, Lorena! Stop being an idiot! I was getting worried!” she complained, and Lorena smiled, forgetting the pain in her abdomen, the discomfort in her chest, her dry mouth, her exhausted body.
When Eduarda smiled back, Lorena knew she had everything she needed right in front of her.

“Look at you, smiling a little,” she pointed out, stretching out her arm and sliding her hand to the back of Eduarda's neck. But when she tried to play with the high collar of the sweater Eduarda wore against the ICU chill—another piece from her Custode line—her fingers caught on the necklace chain.

Lorena had noticed the silver necklace before, but she wasn't sure she could ask about it, or even that she wanted to. This time she tugged gently, watching Eduarda's expression as though asking permission. Eduarda hesitated but didn't stop her, which was enough for Lorena to continue.
When her fingers curled around Eduarda's neck and the front of the jewelry emerged from beneath the cotton threads, Lorena froze, the chain caught between her index and middle fingers.

The ring surfaced like a memory of the past. Of the day Eduarda had knelt in the living room of the apartment they shared with Paulinho, after everything they'd been through together. The day they danced to Farol das Estrelas, as they had so many times before. The day they declared their love and ate mushroom stew, just as they had on so many other nights. The day that had started everything and, in a way, set in motion the ending that would come the following year. The dream that had become a nightmare. The life they'd built together, transformed into an ocean of separation. A ring and a marriage proposal.

For a moment, neither of them dared speak. Lorena was too stunned to form a sentence, in too much pain to move. Eduarda looked away, embarrassed for reasons she didn't understand. When Lorena's trembling, still somewhat unsteady hand caught her chin, Eduarda couldn't bring herself not to meet its owner's eyes. Every effort Lorena made to move her limbs, to touch her, cost so much, and Eduarda wasn't willing to waste her strength.
“Since... since when have you been wearing that?” she stammered. Eduarda let out an audible sigh, knowing she'd been caught red-handed and now had some explaining to do.
“Since the day I told the hospital the truth.” Lorena wanted to count back, but her thoughts were muddled. How long ago had that been? How many weeks? It was hard to tell.
Her fingers slid along the chain until the ring rested in her palm. Not even the cold metal against her skin, made colder by the freezing air-conditioning, could make it feel real.

“I had no idea you'd kept it. I thought...” She hesitated again before continuing. “I thought you'd thrown it away. I don't know, burned it in a bonfire, sold it, donated it.” Lorena listed every possibility that had crossed her mind over those years. She'd be lying if she said she'd never wondered what Eduarda would do with the ring.

“To be honest, I tried.” Eduarda found the courage to answer, wearing a bitter smile at the memory. “I thought about selling it, but it isn't worth much. It's not as if we had a lot of money when I bought it, and I didn't want money from anything that had to do with you.” She swallowed the irony of that sentence, thinking of the car, the twenty million in clothes—a subject for another time. “I thought about giving it away, throwing it into the sea, tossing it in the trash, but I never could. Every time I opened the dresser drawer and it was there, it felt as if something was telling me not to. Maybe that makes sense now. Maybe it was you all along, telling me you'd come back someday. Or maybe I simply never managed to let go.”
Eduarda knew the last possibility was probably closest to the truth. Lorena watched her, turning the ring between her fingers, still unsure what to say.

Knowing that Eduarda still chose to carry her against her chest, around her neck, in her hands, wherever she went, after everything they'd been through—that she'd kept the ring for so long despite having every reason to get rid of it as quickly as possible—was further proof that she held so much more inside than she ever said. Further proof that, at the end of the day, their separation had never truly happened. Not completely. Not even Santiago and all his threats had been enough to break what existed between them. It was perpetual, resilient, eternal, enduring. And at the same time so sensitive it was almost fragile. Yet the feeling was armored, untouchable. No one could interfere with it except the two of them.

“I just needed something that reminded me of you. Some way to take you home with me while you were here, to keep you close. I wouldn't have been able to leave on any of those days otherwise. It sounds silly, but I think it helped me hold on to a little of my sanity. Whenever I missed you, you were right there.”
Eduarda played with the ring, and Lorena watched in silence, feeling their fingers brush as they held the object that represented the life they'd once planned to share.
Lorena glanced around the room, her eyes settling on the small suitcase on the couch. The same one she'd brought on her first day in the hospital, after Eduarda convinced her to begin treatment.

“Would you do me a favor?” she asked. Eduarda nodded, eager for any excuse to take the conversation away from the ring hanging against her chest. “Can you get my bag? I want to show you something.” Without thinking, Eduarda tucked the ring and chain back inside her collar, as if she had to protect them, make sure no one would tear them from her neck the way Santiago had torn Lorena from her life.
Eduarda fetched the suitcase and sat down again. Lorena nodded toward the zipper.
“See if you can find my wallet. I left it in there. I'm not sure if my mom took it out.”

Eduarda hesitated when some part of her subconscious realized where this was going. Even so, she dug into the bag, feeling her way among clothes, towels, and personal belongings Lorena had used since arriving at the hospital, until she found the wallet at the bottom.

Like most of her belongings, the wallet and suitcase were Custode creations. Eduarda looked back at the bed, and Lorena nodded for her to go ahead and open it. It felt like an invasion of privacy. Or perhaps a simple act that helped restore the intimacy they'd once shared, since Eduarda had lost count of the times she'd opened Lorena's wallet, backpack, purse, wardrobe, drawers, and phone when they were together, never needing to ask permission or a password to go through her things.

She stared at the impressive collection of credit cards, most from international banks she'd never even heard of. The old ID, the same one Lorena had always used, still bearing her teenage photograph, brought a smile to Eduarda's face.

That version of Lorena, more than any other, was hers. Entirely hers. The same smile, the same dimple, the crooked front tooth that had grown in wrong after the bicycle accident Leonardo had caused, the same lighthearted gaze, free of any torment. Exactly the same Lorena from the day they'd met. The contrasts were strange and always jarring. Pieces of her old life, proof that she was still the same person, and traces of her new life, of who she'd become while she was away. The Lorena Eduarda still needed to get to know.

The clearest example was her Italian ID, tucked beside the Brazilian document, preserving the duality of those two chapters of her life. Citizenship had been a courtesy, since Lorena hadn't lived in the country long enough to apply for naturalization. In recognition of her services, her involvement with the community, and her prominence in cultural and economic production, Lorena had officially become a citizen the previous year, invited and approved by the highest levels of government.
She was certain it was much more a matter of national pride than anything else.

The country of fashion would never accept that one of its biggest brands had been created and run entirely by a foreigner. If Custode was Italian in origin, marked by the Made in Italy hand-stitched into every label, then Lorena would have to be Italian too. Although she knew the concession wasn't free of strings, she'd accepted it anyway. It spared her a great deal of bureaucracy.

Eduarda remembered hearing about it. The offer of citizenship had become major news in Brazil precisely because it was so unusual. Newspapers and gossip sites had spent weeks explaining just how special Lorena was. But, as with everything involving her, Eduarda had trained her algorithms to label the subject not interested and move on.
But neither the document nor the realization of how many moments in Lorena's life she'd missed was what held her gaze. It was the object tucked into the plastic-covered photo slot.

Eduarda swallowed hard, staring at a ring identical to her own, cared for as lovingly as Lorena had wished, all those years, that she could care for her. She was staring at the wedding band too. The same one she had made herself look at every day since stepping off that plane five years ago.

The ring lay atop a yellowed, folded piece of paper and a photo slightly larger than a passport picture. It showed the two of them. Lorena and Eduarda as they'd been before, smiling and embracing in the middle of a crowd, minutes after their upside-down Spider-Man kiss at the Carnival street party. Lorena wore her black button-down shirt open, her belly covered in glitter and exposed beneath a cropped top. Eduarda had her hair tied back, sweat on her face, the superhero mask hanging from her shoulder. She remembered Maggye taking the picture on her phone. The quality wasn't perfect, but it was one of her favorite photographs of them together.

“I love that photo,” Lorena said with a smile when she noticed how long Eduarda lingered over it. “It's one of my favorites. Remember that board in my bedroom? The one with all our favorite moments?” Eduarda didn't answer because she didn't have the strength, but she remembered. Lorena had a huge metal board above her desk, where she loved choosing and pinning up her favorite photos, not just with Eduarda but with Maggye, Leonardo, and Paulo. As she liked to call it, the five of us corner.

“I took them all to Italy. Sometimes I liked looking at them, sometimes I didn't. It hurt too much. But I had some printed smaller so I could carry them with me. I liked remembering all of you. The way we used to be.” Beside the ring, in a second plastic-covered slot, was a photograph of the group singing happy birthday around the improvised brownie at the burger place they'd fled to after Eduarda's ruined birthday.
Without realizing it, Eduarda moved her hand, tracing Lorena's face in the picture with her index finger.
She'd seen that photo countless times too, and she always noticed that detail.
The way Lorena smiled, clapping as she looked at Eduarda's face. The way the love between them was visible in their eyes. The way Eduarda looked happy on her birthday for the first time.

Lorena had spent five years carrying those photographs in her wallet, traveling from country to country, giving important interviews, meeting celebrities, presidents, even the Pope at a Mass in St. Peter's Square to which she'd been invited despite her sexuality. She always lingered a little longer when taking out a card, when handing over her ID to board a flight. Her eyes always drifted to them. The great loves of her life. Not just Eduarda, but Paulo and Leonardo. And still, above all, Eduarda.
The thought made Eduarda's chest ache. Lorena didn't deserve that kind of loneliness. If she had anything to say about it, Lorena would never feel alone again. She looked at the ring once more.

“It was the only piece of you I had left. The only tangible part of you in my life,” Lorena tried to explain, her voice shaking beneath a sad smile. “If you couldn't get rid of yours, imagine how I felt. I think I needed to take you with me too, to have something that reminded me of you. I wouldn't have survived a single day in that place without it.”

It took Eduarda a moment to understand that that place meant Italy. A place Lorena had, in her own way, learned to love, learned to call home, even learned to call her country. A place that could be a dream, filled with immeasurable beauty, but would never have Eduarda in it. And that was enough to turn it into a prison.
Eduarda looked up, silently asking permission, and Lorena nodded. There was no point hiding anything anymore.

Carefully, she picked up the folded sheet, recognizing the sentences and the handwriting the moment she read them, words on one side and more on the back. Their promises. The things they'd celebrated together.
Having someone to go to vegan restaurants with.
Finding out what it feels like to fall in love and realizing every day how lucky I am to have found a first love who is everything I ever wanted.
Trying to be as good to you as you are to me. Every single day.
Eduarda didn't realize she was crying until the first drop landed on a curve of black ink.
“I can't... believe you kept this.” Lorena nodded, holding her hand.

“There's a huge box in my walk-in closet filled with things that belong to us. Ten years of memories, and I've never had the courage to open it again. But I've never had the courage to get rid of anything, either. It was the first thing I packed when I had to leave.” Eduarda was still staring at the paper, not knowing what to say or think. But it wasn't all that surprising.

Her chest tightened at an image she'd never allowed herself to imagine. Lorena, devastated, alone, frightened, threatened, abandoned by the person who should have protected her. Even so, she'd found the strength to pack her things, board a plane without saying goodbye, and start a new life alone in another country. And now she was still fighting.

Eduarda placed the paper on the bedside table and set the ring on top to keep it from blowing away. The suitcase fell to the floor as she moved her legs, and the wallet lay abandoned on the mattress. None of it mattered now, however much it meant. What mattered was the certainty that she'd never admired Lorena's strength so much, loved her heart so deeply, or wanted every part of her so fiercely.

She leaned closer to the bed, but this time she didn't lie down. She rested her forehead against Lorena's, thinking of all the kisses she wanted to give but couldn't. Eduarda wanted to cover her in kisses. From head to toe. To worship every inch of her, every part that would forever hold all of her love.
“I love you so much,” she whispered, closing her eyes, feeling as if her chest might burst.
Eduarda silently promised herself that she would never let anyone hurt Lorena like that again. Like Zenilda, she would never allow Santiago near her again.

If she could, she'd keep Lorena from feeling any pain. She would personally make sure that, however much time they had—months, years, decades—Lorena felt loved every second. Because that was what she deserved. What she needed. She would never be alone again.
Lorena smiled and let her tired head sink into the pillow. Their conversation had exhausted her.
“I love you too. I'm sorry I scared you.” Eduarda nodded, her own strength fading.

With the blanket and suitcase still on the floor, the wallet on the mattress, one wedding band hanging against Eduarda's chest and the other resting on a paper filled with promises they were still trying to keep, they fell asleep together. For the first time in a week, Eduarda managed to rest.

The first week brought a harsh dose of reality. Lorena knew she was weak, knew recovery would be difficult, but only as time passed and her body grew increasingly limited and dependent did she begin to grasp the true extent of her condition.

During the first days, she barely felt human. Her nutrition remained tied to intravenous access, and daily meals disappeared from her routine. She couldn't move without help, and often not even with it. Every physical therapy session, whether to improve her breathing or fight muscle atrophy, came in small acts of torture, because her entire body hurt all the time.

Breathing hurt her chest, still tender from resuscitation. Even the simplest movements—trying to lift a leg or tolerate a gradual increase in the angle of her hospital bed—demanded superhuman energy. Without ever getting up, every hour she was made to exercise ended with her forehead coated in cold sweat, her hands shaking, and her body drained.
Lorena always slept for hours afterward, gradually noticing that there was no longer a comfortable position in the bed with her aching back. Then she woke, and the whole thing started again.

Still, on some days she wished pain were the worst part. She thought the hardest part of being hospitalized was behind her, until she came face to face with the brutal reality of postoperative recovery.
More than the physical battle, the vulnerability of being in that condition made her cry at night, when she was alone, and in her most fragile moments, in front of Eduarda.
Lorena felt embarrassed all the time by her inability to do the most basic things.

Unable to get up to use the bathroom, she had to have her teeth brushed in bed. Her urine was drained through a catheter, and her bowel movements were collected in the adult diapers she was forced to wear, which only made her feel more helpless and humiliated at once. Unable to bathe, she was washed right there in the bed, in a makeshift cleaning with wet wipes, towels, water, and soap. The nurses were always willing to help, and that was what they were there for. It was part of their job. Even so, it was the part of her ICU days she hated most.

Sometimes Eduarda offered to help, and Lorena couldn't decide which was worse. Being treated like a helpless newborn by strangers, or by the woman who knew her as more than that, who had fallen in love with a different Lorena. Alive, independent, happy. In the end she always gave in to Eduarda's well-aimed tenderness and her insistent pleas to be patient.

Before she knew it, Eduarda would be there, holding the metal basin for her to spit out her toothpaste. Offering water to rinse her mouth. Helping gently wipe her body with towels while chatting with her throughout, distracting her from what was happening.

She was there whenever she could be, turning on the television with the sound muted to a program she knew Lorena would like. Stroking her face until she slept. Holding her hand and wiping her tears when Cristina needed two nurses to help turn her onto her side and collect another bone marrow aspirate, the test she hated most.

It wasn't the thick needle piercing her hip that bothered her this time. It was the searing pain in her abdomen when they had to move her. The pain that accompanied everything she did, that never went away.

For Eduarda, it was an obvious decision. Part of her promises. For Lorena, it was a challenge to accept a reality in which she'd surrendered so completely to her own weakness. A reality where Eduarda saw her at her absolute worst every day and found every possible reason to fall out of love. To everyone else, it was simply another of the countless sincere gestures of love flowing between them.

A week after extubation, Lorena was struggling with the first attempt to reintroduce food. For now, only soft, puréed meals: porridge, mashed vegetables and fruit, soups, creamy dishes, and smoothies. Before, she'd thought the worst would be the weeks of chemotherapy, when the mere smell of a meal made her want to vomit.

Eduarda sat in the armchair beside her, patient as always, with a calm and tenderness that sometimes made Lorena wonder where she found them. She stretched a hand toward the tray resting over Lorena, gathering a little mashed arracacha onto the tip of the spoon.
“Just a little more, come on, babe,” she pleaded. Lorena hated herself every time she couldn't answer the entreaties in that gentle voice. “You've had four spoonfuls.”

It wasn't a demand, much less a scolding. It was simply a remark that made her worry clear. Parenteral nutrition would continue until Lorena could eat enough to sustain herself again. But she wouldn't get there without taking these tiny steps.

Eduarda sighed when she saw her expression. Empty, in a way that was becoming more common, and that frightened her. Sometimes she saw sadness, frustration, fear, pain—feelings that belonged to the process. Other times, on the worst days, she saw nothing at all.
Worried, Eduarda set the spoon aside and carefully rested her hand on Lorena's abdomen.
“Tell me what you're feeling,” she asked again, giving Lorena her full attention.

The truth was that Lorena needed a therapy session much more than food forced down her throat. Eduarda picked up the tray, moving the meal out of sight in the hope that distancing Lorena from this tangible reminder of her limitations would help her speak. Lorena sighed. Eduarda had explicitly asked her to be honest about her symptoms. Now she had to be.
“My stomach hurts,” she admitted, closing her eyes and sinking into the pillow, feeling the bed raised a little higher so she could eat without choking.
Her throat still felt raw when she spoke. Lorena still had to stop, breathe, and cough between sentences to keep from running out of air. Her voice was still weak, but Eduarda always listened.
“Where?” she asked in a clinical tone Lorena might have loved at another time.

At least, she used to love finding traces of Doctor Eduarda in everyday life. In casual conversations about someone's health, in the stories she told about her patients. Now Lorena only wished she never had to hear another oncology question come out of her mouth.
She moved her hands to the center of her belly, over the pit of her stomach, and Eduarda nodded.

“That's normal. You haven't eaten solid food in more than two weeks. Your stomach is going to react. But we have to get through it. Your body needs to adjust again.” There it was, the plural once more. The way Eduarda spoke that made Lorena believe this was a team effort rather than a battle she was fighting alone. “Just one more spoonful. Please. Then I'll stop bugging you,” she insisted. Lorena took a deep breath, wondering if she'd ever develop the ability to refuse a request from that mouth.

With no choice, she agreed, watching Eduarda turn back to the tray and put a careful portion on the spoon. Not too full, not too empty. Even so, Lorena stared at it as though it were a mountain miles high when Eduarda brought it to her lips, holding her now-unsplinted hand underneath to make sure nothing spilled on the blankets. Lorena sighed as the smell of food triggered an immediate reaction in her stomach, which churned, sending up a wave of nausea.

Still, she opened her mouth and accepted it, the purée lingering far too long before she forced herself to swallow. Her eyes closed and watered as Lorena tried to breathe slowly, unable to understand how something so simple had become so difficult. A touch at the corner of her mouth brought her back. Eduarda was wiping it with a napkin, leaving a gentle caress on her cheek before turning away to gather the trash on the tray.
“We're doing well. Today was five spoonfuls. Tomorrow it'll be six. Everything's going to be okay.”
Lorena neither denied nor agreed. She only sighed, feeling utterly spent.

Eduarda studied her, as she'd been learning to do more and more often over the past few weeks. If she'd once been an expert at reading Lorena's eyes, she was becoming an expert at reading her silences. They came more frequently now, longer, more mysterious and profound. Sometimes a shadow fell over her gaze, darkening even the pale green that reflected the sea.
It was a kind of sadness Eduarda had never seen in Lorena before. The only person who would recognize it was Maggye, who'd lived with that emptiness on Lorena's face for five years.

With time, its presence had faded, but it always returned at some point. On special days, birthdays, during the holidays, at major Custode events and achievements, on dates that mattered to their relationship. Or, in the worst moments, on ordinary days. In the kitchen, at dinner, in the early hours of the morning, halfway through a movie, on car rides.

After years of watching this happen, Eduarda knew it was impossible to spend so much time in a hospital and not change somehow. Lorena was changing. Recovery from this surgery was demanding a far higher price than any she'd paid before. The limitations, the pain, the prison of the bed and the medication, the inability to manage even the most basic bodily needs. It was a combination slowly and visibly draining Lorena. And it worried her.

“Hey,” she said, leaning closer and sighing as she rested a hand against Lorena's cheek. Lorena's eyes closed again, a breath of relief escaping her mouth, as if Eduarda's touch were all she needed. “Talk to me. I don't like seeing you this quiet. You can give everyone else one-word answers, but not when it's just the two of us. I've already gone too long without hearing your voice.” It was emotional blackmail, and Lorena knew it.

She looked at Eduarda, tired of seeing that same worried expression behind that damned mask that always kept her from seeing her entire face. Just like the face she loved most, visible only from the eyes up, her life felt that way now too. Half of what it had been.

“Just... I don't know, distract me for a bit,” Lorena asked, feeling as though her mind might shut down completely if she spent another second in that room, in that bed. “Tell me about the days I was unconscious. Are you okay? Did I miss anything important?”

Eduarda stopped, her mouth slightly open, hesitating at the irony of Lorena asking about precisely the part she most wanted to avoid. A stifled laugh escaped through her nose. And however far from her best Lorena might be, Eduarda would always be a part of her life that made sense. A part of her life in which no detail would go unnoticed.
“What is it?” Lorena asked, frowning, and Eduarda immediately regretted her spontaneous reaction. “Why did you make that face? What happened?”
Lorena tried to move, only to be struck once again by the visceral pain deep in her abdomen. Eduarda reacted instinctively, reaching out both hands to hold her still.

“Babe, stop. You're still not well enough for that.” Eduarda cursed herself for not hiding her reaction better. Lorena had missed some important events. Including an attempted visit from her father, which wasn't on the list of things Eduarda intended to reveal. Still, Lorena was staring at her with that worried, determined expression of someone who wasn't about to give up easily.

“Eduarda, if you don't tell me what happened, I'll find a way to find out myself, and it'll cost me a lot more time and, most importantly, energy.” If Eduarda had her methods of emotional blackmail, Lorena had hers too. She knew she'd won the argument when Eduarda closed her eyes, sighed, and rubbed her forehead.

“I can tell you, but I don't want you getting worked up. If that damn thing starts going off, you're lying back down and going to sleep,” she said authoritatively, pointing to the monitor that was still tracking Lorena's heart rate in real time. The threat hung unanswered as they stared each other down, each waiting for the other to give in to the silence.

Lorena would never admit how much she loved it when Eduarda spoke to her that way, ready to take charge of her entire life. And Eduarda would never admit that she was always the one who ended up obeying.

“I gave a statement to the hospital board about the two of us,” she said all at once. Lorena swallowed hard, trying to steady her breathing, with no doubt Eduarda would actually end the conversation if she got too upset. “It went fine, before you ask. I told the truth and defended myself as best I could. Paulo and Gerluce helped me go through the Medical Code of Ethics looking for good arguments, and frankly I don't think the Regional Medical Council has much they can use against me. But the board is still going to vote on whether to refer the case, and I wouldn't be surprised if they approve it.”
The monitor kept beeping at the same steady pace. Lorena listened without any dramatic reaction.
“And did it really go okay?” she asked. Eduarda nodded. Any trouble she might face with the hospital seemed so small after nearly losing Lorena.

“It did. It was tiring and stressful, mostly because they kept wasting my time when I wanted to be with you, but...” Eduarda stopped, biting her lip when she realized Lorena would find out anyway. She and Zenilda couldn't keep her away from screens forever. “There were two complicating factors that might become a problem.”
Lorena fell silent, staring at her and waiting for an answer. Eduarda sighed before continuing.

“Couldn't you at least have warned me that the clothes you sent to my house were worth twenty million reais, Lorena?” There it was: her full name, no babe, no softening the blow. Lorena frowned, not understanding the problem.

“How much did you think they were worth?” she asked with as much of a shrug as she could manage. “I sent you everything Custode currently sells. And in my defense, it wasn't just clothes. There were shoes and handbags and accessories, and you still insist on wearing those fucking Crocs.” Lorena pointed at the floor without needing to look at Eduarda's feet to see them.

“That's your argument? Going after my Crocs?” Eduarda shot back, unable to suppress a crooked smile, because she'd missed this. The everyday complaints, this version of Lorena who watched her with fire in her eyes and a sharp sense of humor, ready to turn any argument around. Not the woman who spent hours in silence staring at the ceiling and the television.

“What do you want me to do?” Lorena insisted. “Lower the price of the clothes just so you won't feel bad? In my defense, Custode prices are in euros, so thirty million would be, what? Less than five million?” Eduarda sighed, unsure where to begin.
“I said twenty million, not thirty,” she corrected. Lorena looked at her without moving.

“Fine. But they estimated it wrong. Custode's current catalog, including shoes, bags, and accessories, is worth thirty million reais, not twenty. More precisely, twenty-nine million, eight hundred and thirty-seven reais and twenty-three centavos. Last time I checked.”
Eduarda didn't know whether to swear or be impressed by Lorena's ability to remember even the cents after spending a week sedated. At least that was a good sign.

“Seriously, Lorena?! Seriously?! Thirty million...” Eduarda cut herself off, unable to understand how thirty million reais' worth of clothing could possibly fit in her walk-in closet. And accessories. Thirty million reais shouldn't fit in a closet. Or an apartment. It was more than enough money to pay off her mortgage dozens of times.

She could end hunger in entire cities, fund research, give half away, and still live out the rest of her life on investment income. It was an inconceivable amount of money to Eduarda. The kind of money that apparently amounted to pocket change for Lorena. She gazed into the eyes that had once belonged to the eighteen-year-old girl she'd met, gradually realizing that, deep down, she was dealing with someone new. A woman she didn't fully know. A woman far more powerful than Eduarda could ever have imagined Lorena Ferette would become.
“What am I supposed to do with you?” she asked, at a loss for words. Lorena had an answer.

“Well, you could start by retiring your Crocs and wearing my shoes. Do you have some kind of problem with Custode's designs? If you want, I can design an entire collection perfectly molded to your feet and have them made for you. They'll be a lot more comfortable than that piece of shit—sorry, piece of plastic—you wear.”
Eduarda laughed, perhaps the first genuine laugh to escape her lips in more than a week. She looked at Lorena with a half-smile. At least the distraction was working.

“You could do a collaboration. Custode + Crocs. Custocrocs. It'd be a worldwide hit. Imagine a whole range of lesbian-green Crocs with little four-leaf-clover charms.” She pushed her luck further, watching Lorena's face crumple as if she'd been personally insulted.
“Wow. I think I'd rather die,” Lorena replied casually, until she realized what she'd just said. Eduarda's smile vanished, and silence fell between them.
It was just an expression, she knew. Even so, it sounded completely different now. Lorena took Eduarda's hand, and Eduarda looked down at their intertwined fingers.
“Duda, I'm sorry, I...” she began, but Eduarda shook her head.
“It's okay. I know what you meant.” Even so, her voice had grown weaker, and a serious, distant expression replaced the almost lighthearted conversation they'd managed to have.
That was how Eduarda felt. As if that subject hovered over them constantly, swept under the rug because the possibility was too painful for anyone to face.

But it would surface without warning, like a punch to the stomach, a bullet to the chest, the sharp pain of stubbing your little toe on the corner of a piece of furniture, all because of a phrase said without thinking. The heavy breathing of death threatening to draw near drained everything of meaning. Every chance Eduarda had to be completely happy seemed to require a guarantee that the threat would never come near Lorena again.

“Why are you asking about the price of the clothes? Did they say something about that?” Lorena asked gently, trying to caress Eduarda with her words because she couldn't do much with her hands. Eduarda looked up and sighed.

“I don't want you feeling guilty.” A terrible way to start. “But technically, the gifts you gave me could be considered a financial benefit obtained through an inappropriate doctor-patient relationship. That is in the code of ethics, and they could use it against me. Most doctors receive gifts from patients. It's relatively normal. But twenty—well, thirty million is pretty damn hard to explain.”
Lorena froze, trying to process the information that had caught her off guard. Whatever Eduarda was about to say, it was too late. Lorena already felt guilty, and not a little.
“Duda, I'm sorry. I had absolutely no idea that could...” Before she could finish, Eduarda moved, leaning toward the bed and taking hold of her chin.

“Stop that. I'm serious. If even I, who know the code of ethics, never considered that it could be a problem, how could you have known?” she said firmly, seeing in Lorena's eyes that convincing her wouldn't be easy. “I don't want you feeling bad. Not for a second, because...” Eduarda hesitated, smiling when she realized she knew exactly where to strike.

“I'm not going to regret accepting your clothes. Even if I think thirty million is absurdly excessive. Even if the amounts make me uncomfortable, ethics code or no ethics code. It's Custode, and Custode is your life. You created Custode for me, babe. Do you really think I care what a board full of Faria Lima corporate types decides that means? The only thing I see in it, the only thing that matters, is your love.”

Lorena's eyes filled with tears, not from fear, sadness, or worry about what might happen to Eduarda. It was the realization that, five years later, she'd done it. Eduarda understood what Custode meant. But she was wrong about one thing.

“Custode isn't my life. You are,” she replied with such certainty that Eduarda couldn't stop her smile. She glanced away, a little embarrassed, before looking at Lorena again and stroking her chin with her fingertips.
Her eyes blinked slowly, savoring every second before she had to leave. It was always like this. Their afternoons together passed far too quickly, and the nights seemed to have no end.
“How am I supposed to stay pissed at you when you say things like that?” Eduarda whispered.

“You don't have to be,” Lorena replied, and Eduarda shook her head. Still, she smiled, letting her gaze linger on Lorena's face, because she knew she'd miss her the moment she left the hospital. Her daily torment was going home and having to sleep alone.

“Babe, I need to show you something, but you have to keep your promise not to get upset,” Eduarda went on, sighing as she remembered her earlier conversation with Zenilda. Lorena would find out sooner or later, and it was better that she didn't find out on her own.
Lorena frowned, not upset but worried. Eduarda's hesitant expression didn't help. The beeping sped up slightly, and both of them turned toward the monitor.

Slowly, the rhythm of the lines began to ease again. Lorena watched silently as Eduarda sighed and took her phone from her pocket. Lorena's own was in her mother's custody, on the strange grounds that phones were among the greatest carriers of bacteria passing from human hand to human hand and that Lorena had to avoid contamination at all costs. A sentence that sounded as if Eduarda herself had written it, not Zenilda, who certainly wouldn't have thought of that.

The article was already open. The same one Eduarda had read in full, detailing Lorena's condition and spreading rumors about their relationship. She stared at the headline, the photograph of the hospital, an old photo from Lorena's Instagram that made her grateful she'd spent five years avoiding news about her, because Lorena looked like an Italian goddess descended from the heavens. Eduarda slowly handed over the phone. Lorena looked up, a question in her eyes, and received a nod in return. Permission to go ahead.

Lorena read slowly, struggling to absorb each word and discovering more limits to her body even in simple tasks. The weight of the phone in her hand made her arm ache as if she were holding several pounds. Her fingers were still too uncoordinated to scroll smoothly. The blue light bothered her as much as, perhaps more than, the harsh ICU lights. Even her reading speed felt strange. Lorena felt like a child learning to read all over again. The time it took her to read the article was twice what it would have been on a normal day. Even so, she read to the end.
When she finished, she let her head fall against the pillow and raised a hand to her forehead.
“Oh, for fuck's sake, Duda. I'm so sorry,” Lorena said, feeling guilty again.

She wasn't worried about any leak concerning her health or whether she was being portrayed as close to death. For several days, she really had been, and it made no difference whether the public knew it. But what they were saying about Eduarda did matter.

Realizing how naive she'd been, Lorena moved, opening Eduarda's phone browser. Eduarda didn't stop her. Lorena typed her own name, getting several letters wrong because her fingers weren't moving accurately. The search worked anyway, and a long list of articles in other languages appeared. All followed the same line as the first, mentioning her condition, Eduarda's name, and the hospital. In English, French, Italian, German, even a few in Japanese and Korean.
It always happened that way. The first leak was only the beginning. A flood inevitably followed.

“Sorry for what?” Eduarda asked firmly as she watched Lorena's expression grow even more distant. She took the phone from Lorena's hands and set it on the table. “Did you write it? Did you leak it? Besides, I'm pretty sure the hospital lawyers are shitting themselves at the thought of you suing.” Lorena's eyes widened, and she frowned.

“Of course I'm not going to sue. Do you think I'll waste my time on that?” But then she replayed the words hospital lawyers. “They didn't give you trouble over this, did they?” Lorena asked, putting two and two together. “The board.”
Eduarda bit her lip, and Lorena knew the answer before she even gave it.

“It came out the day before my hearing, so the timing couldn't have been worse. They didn't dwell on it too much, but obviously my relationship with you hurts São Peregrino's image once people portray it as something clandestine. It makes it look as if the hospital can't control its own staff. So, one way or another, it gives them grounds to argue that my failure to disclose our relationship had negative consequences for the institution.” Lorena slowly rubbed her face, unsure what to say as exhaustion from the conversation finally overwhelmed her body. She opened her mouth, but Eduarda cut her off.

“If you apologize for turning my life into a mess again, I'm going to be genuinely upset.” She got there first, making air quotes with her fingers as she said mess. Lorena rolled her eyes toward her, wondering how Eduarda knew exactly what she was about to say before she'd even uttered the first syllable.
“Haven't you figured out yet that this is the only mess I want, babe?” she asked with a smile, her thumb circling gently around Lorena's eye. Lorena sighed.

“If being with you makes me a somewhat public figure, I don't care. Aren't I your first lady? Wasn't that what you wrote in that letter? Unless you're embarrassed to be seen with me, because God knows you must've had plenty of chances to hook up with Italian women who were much prettier and hotter than me, I'm available and ready to take the role.
