Or do you really think the first lady of Custode's owner is going to go unnoticed?”
Lorena let a smile slip out, still feeling guilty, but Eduarda had that gift. She was one of the few people who could make Lorena smile in that place.

For a moment, she let herself imagine it. A reality where she could bring Eduarda with her everywhere, on every trip, to every event and fashion show. Where Eduarda would want to take up the role she'd always held in Lorena's life. Lorena imagined the articles they'd write about them, about a relationship so many would envy. Features in major lifestyle magazines. Television crews visiting her home on Lake Como to show how she and Eduarda lived. The privilege of finally saying publicly that she'd been in love for as long as she could remember and was in a committed relationship, as she'd avoided doing in every interview where they asked about her personal life. It was the kind of inevitable exposure she'd love, as long as it let her show Eduarda to the world. Eduarda deserved to be seen. Admired.

“Are you really going to keep bringing up all those hypothetical Italian women I supposedly slept with?” Lorena asked with a laugh, wondering if Eduarda would ever understand that she'd never be able to be with anyone else as long as her heart belonged to her, which it always would. “And I'm not even going to answer that part about being ashamed to be seen with you. My doctor says I'm not allowed to get worked up.” Eduarda smiled back, noticing that Lorena meant her, not Cristina.

“But, just so we're clear, I didn't write that you were my first lady. I wrote that you were my eternal first lady. There's a difference,” Lorena pointed out, and Eduarda laughed, continuing to caress her face while studying her expressions with the determination of someone intent on finding something. And she always found it.

It was obvious that simply spending so much time talking, even lying down, was exhausting her again. The way she closed her eyes and furrowed her brow every time she felt pain in the surgical area. Or raised her hand to her forehead every time she swallowed a little saliva, still feeling discomfort from the intubation.
When Lorena moved her tongue around her lips a few times, Eduarda picked up the cup.

“Come here.” She leaned closer as she did every day, gently holding Lorena's chin and bringing over the cup of water she'd already prepared. Lorena didn't deny her thirst, but she took a few careful sips, which cost her as much effort as the spoonfuls of purée. She touched Eduarda's arm when she'd had enough, judging more by how much pain her throat could bear than by the still overwhelming urge to drink an entire bottle to ease her dry mouth.
Eduarda was content with another small step forward, setting the cup back on the bedside table while Lorena took advantage of the contact to run her thumb playfully over Eduarda's wrist.
“I wanted my little sparkling water,” she grumbled. Eduarda smiled at the affectionate diminutive.
“Not yet, babe. Nothing that might make your abdomen more uncomfortable.” Lorena didn't argue. She simply relaxed and closed her eyes, as if going to sleep.

Eduarda didn't doubt she needed rest and, although she knew Lorena's disrupted sleep had become a game of Russian roulette and there was a good chance she wouldn't wake in time for them to say goodbye at the end of visiting hours, Eduarda still preferred that she sleep.

She was beginning to think of taking a nap herself as the minutes stretched out and Lorena's breathing slowly calmed. First, wanting to be sure she really fell asleep, she stayed where she was, studying Lorena's face, offering another of her tender caresses across her cheeks, around her eyes, along her forehead and eyebrows.

Everything seemed peaceful when Lorena opened her heavy eyes again. Eduarda smiled, but instantly noticed the tears gathered there. One slid quietly down, and she wiped it away with the tip of her middle finger. Every day was much the same. Lorena was okay for a while when they talked and let herself be distracted. But the moment silence came and left room for thought, the sadness returned. Eduarda preferred not to imagine what her nights were like when she was alone. It was one of the reasons leaving was always so hard.
“Duda,” she called weakly, and Eduarda was ready.
“Hi, babe,” she practically whispered, not wanting Lorena to lose her sleepiness.

But Lorena shifted, trying to sit a little more upright, at least as far as her body would allow. Eduarda hurried to help, slipping an arm behind her back and listening to Lorena's sighs of pain, unable to tell what was bothering her most: her back, her weak muscles, or her abdomen.
“Do you really think I'm going to get out of here?” The question was vague, and Eduarda couldn't tell whether Lorena meant the hospital or the ICU. But her answer was the same.
“Of course you will. What kind of question is that?” It shouldn't even have been in doubt. But Eduarda understood.

“I know it's hard, but we have to take it one day at a time, one challenge at a time. First you need to get well enough to leave this ICU and go back to a regular room. I miss sleeping with you. I hate having to go home every day.” It was true, and Lorena smiled, clearly thinking of something beyond Eduarda's words.

“If I get well enough to go back to a room, will you promise to spend one night in bed with me?” she pleaded, her lips forming a little pout. “Just one night. I miss falling asleep cuddled up with you so much. And I want kisses. Lots of kisses.”
Eduarda couldn't help smiling too. But she knew it wasn't so simple.

“Babe, I miss all of that like crazy too, but I can't. Your stitches haven't dissolved yet, your abdomen is still very sensitive, and you know I move around like crazy in my sleep. I'm not going to risk kicking you by accident.” Lorena pouted even more, and Eduarda laughed. “And as for the kisses, I swear, I promise that when you get out of here, I'm going to kiss you so much you'll get sick of me and beg me to stop. But I'm not risking passing you any bacteria right now.” Lorena whined in a petulant little voice that, at any other time, would have made Eduarda give her everything she asked for.

“Kisses would be such good motivation to finish this bland purée.” She looked at the plate, still more than half full, and Eduarda narrowed her eyes at yet another round of emotional blackmail. “But since you can't, fine. Let me just say now that dating a doctor is a pain in the ass. Why do you have to be so sensible all the time?”
Lorena didn't notice what she'd said, and Eduarda bit her lip, unable to help herself.
“Oh, really? I had no idea dating me for ten years was so unbearable,” she teased, returning to the familiar caress over Lorena's eyebrow that Lorena loved both giving and receiving.

“To be fair, you only graduated halfway through our relationship, so you weren't officially a doctor for the first five years.” Eduarda didn't respond, still caught on Lorena's earlier words, not sure whether to bring up the subject, even though it hardly mattered.

“And now?” she murmured, suddenly unsure of herself. “I didn't realize we were dating again, for you to go around saying you're dating a doctor. I don't remember hearing anyone ask me, Lorena Ferette.” Lorena stopped and stared at her. Silence settled between them again, and neither broke eye contact, as if they were competing to see who would blink and give in first.

It was strange, Eduarda thought. She hadn't expected a label, a request to be her girlfriend, whatever it might be. Part of her didn't like the idea of taking two steps back and dating Lorena again when, before they'd separated, they'd practically been married. But it was hard to imagine a world in which they could simply pick up exactly where they'd left off and start talking about marriage as though nothing had happened. She didn't care much about naming what they had, because it already had a name. Love. They loved each other and they were together, and that was enough.
Even so, Lorena moved, looking at the chain Eduarda now wore outside the collar, over her clothes, because she no longer needed to hide it.

She reached both hands toward Eduarda, who only understood what she wanted when her unsteady fingers tried to turn the necklace and open the clasp she'd pulled to the front. But her coordination and strength were still completely off, and stretching far enough to reach Eduarda's neck strained the stitches from her surgery.
Not wanting to prolong it, Eduarda stepped in, gently moving Lorena's hands aside.

“Wait. I'll take it off for you,” she said, still not entirely sure what Lorena wanted, though she had her suspicions. Watching her struggle with something so simple hurt. Eduarda couldn't just sit there. So she took off the necklace and placed it in Lorena's hands.
Lorena stared at it for several seconds, still unable to believe Eduarda had really kept it. Then she took her hand, and Eduarda was already smiling beneath her mask.
“Well, let's fix that,” Lorena began. “Eduarda Kamiński Fragoso, would you, by any chance, agree to be my girlfriend again, after these five years that should never have happened?”

Eduarda felt tears begin to run down her face before Lorena had finished the sentence. She hated being like this, so quick to cry, but she couldn't help it. Not after everything they'd been through, everything they were still going through. Not after spending years convinced she'd never see her again, convinced Lorena had never loved her. Hearing those words erased the negative feelings that had haunted her memories of Lorena. It made their fresh start official.

“I know the timing is awful and the circumstances are even worse. I know you deserve more. You deserve a romantic date, an expensive restaurant, a sunset by the pool, by the sea, over the city. A public declaration of love. Not a proposal like this, in an ICU, in a hospital bed. But I don't want to spend another day not knowing for certain that I'm yours.”
Eduarda shook her head, afraid she wouldn't be able to speak.
“I don't care about any of that, babe. Absolutely none of it. I just need you.”

Her voice trembled as a sob escaped, and Lorena smiled for real, perhaps for the first time since she'd been extubated. Slowly, with shaky, unsteady hands, she slipped the ring onto Eduarda's right hand, knowing she wanted more. She wanted the marriage they'd never had, wanted to call her wife. She wanted to reclaim everything they'd lost. But just as Eduarda had described her recovery, it was a process. Slow, one day at a time. And Lorena wanted to savor every detail, every step. Learning again, day after day, what it meant to have Eduarda back.

When the band settled onto her ring finger, Eduarda stretched out the fingers that had only recently healed from their fracture, holding them with her other hand to admire a sight she'd seen every day for more than a year. For a moment, everything seemed to be back in its rightful place. Almost everything, she thought, looking at Lorena. At the line in her collarbone that never seemed to come out, the electrodes on her chest, the oxygen cannula in her nose. One last detail, one last barrier before they could live the life they'd always dreamed of together. Lorena had to heal.

“Are you asking me to be your girlfriend with our engagement ring?” Eduarda asked, still staring at the band. Lorena took her hand and slowly brought it to her mouth, pressing a perfect kiss onto the jewelry before her lips moved to Eduarda's skin. Eduarda might not want to kiss her, but Lorena would kiss her every second she could. Here and forever.
“Don't worry,” Lorena said with a slightly smug smile. “Now I have the money to buy a much bigger diamond for when we get married.”

Eduarda let out a loud, nervous laugh, afraid of what Lorena might come up with if they had that opportunity again. She wanted to say yes, to shout that she accepted, that more than anything she wanted to marry her. But she took a deep breath, turning the ring on her finger as she tried to get used to it again.

Everything was peaceful, and that seemed like a dangerous thought. Later, Eduarda left the ICU the way she did every night, saying goodbye to Lorena with a weight in her chest at having to leave her, especially now that she was beginning to understand just how emotionally shaken Lorena was becoming.

She didn't sleep well, alone in bed, because she'd never managed to relearn how to sleep alone. Eduarda still worried, still overthought everything, still feared the nights apart, the emergency phone calls, the possibility that Lorena might need her in the middle of the night.
But when she closed her eyes, still turning the ring back and forth, she felt happy.

“So, are we going to talk about that ring on your finger?” Gerluce asked the next day as they drove home from the hospital. Eduarda was driving distractedly, as always, thinking of Lorena and replaying every small moment they'd shared during the hours she was allowed in the ICU. Gerluce had finished another shift and was slowly trying to return to her routine as things settled down. Eduarda slowed for the heavy traffic and sighed.

“Talk about what?” Her deliberately casual question made Gerluce lower the phone she'd been studying with her head bent down. She stared at Eduarda, her face showing exactly what she thought of her friend's nerve. The ring was simple, nothing extravagant, bought with difficulty using money Eduarda had saved from her residency stipend, back when she, Lorena, and Paulinho were still struggling to pay the bills in Tatuapé. But it was beautiful, and it meant something.

A thin, delicate white-gold band, her favorite kind of jewelry, with a solitary diamond at the center, so small it was almost easy to miss. Eduarda watched the contrast of the silvery shine against the steering wheel and sighed. She hadn't been able to stop looking at it since she put it on.
“Duda, do you think we're stupid? Everyone's noticed. Zenilda, Maggye, Paulo, Léo,” Gerluce shot back. Eduarda shrugged as though it didn't matter.

“And you drew the short straw and had to ask?” she teased. Gerluce took a deep breath, unable to understand why Eduarda was being so difficult. But even in the dim car, she could make out her friend's smile, barely contained by a bite to the inside of her cheek. It looked genuine, and Gerluce tried, but couldn't remember the last time she'd seen her smile that way.

“Are you going to make me beg, Eduarda?” she complained sarcastically. Eduarda laughed as she stopped at a red light. She let her head fall against the padded seat, closed her eyes, and kept smiling. Her cheeks were starting to ache a little; her heart was fluttering in exactly the right way, excited like a teenager falling in love for the first time all over again. Eduarda could feel herself blushing, but she couldn't bring herself to care.

“I don't know. What do you want me to say?” She glanced at Gerluce. “I wasn't worried about it. About a label or anything. I think Lorena and I moved past needing to name things a long time ago, and that's okay. But we were talking, and she found out I'd been wearing our engagement ring on a necklace. One thing sort of led to another, and before I knew it she was asking me to be her girlfriend again.”
Gerluce went still, confused by so much information at once.

“Wait. Are you telling me that ring...?” She pointed at Eduarda's hand just as the light turned green. The car accelerated, and for a moment Eduarda forgot that Gerluce was the only person they'd mentioned who had never seen that ring before.
“It's the ring I bought to propose to Lorena. I kept mine. She kept hers, too. We talked about it. And suddenly I was saying yes to being with her all over again.”

Gerluce couldn't help smiling too. It was contagious. It wasn't just that she'd never seen Eduarda smile like that. She'd never seen Eduarda happy like that. And that was saying a lot, considering the situation still hanging over everything involving Lorena.
“Did it bother you?” Gerluce asked. Eduarda frowned, not understanding. “Having to sort of start dating again when you two should already be married?”
She shook her head, turning the wheel to begin heading down toward Ibirapuera.

“Not really. It's a little strange, yes. But I think Lorena and I need to go through those stages, you know? It's part of it, and that's okay. I want to enjoy every stage with her all over again. And as soon as she gets better, I'm going to ask that woman to marry me, Gerluce. I swear to God.”

Gerluce didn't doubt her for a second. She reached across to stroke her friend's arm in support, unsure whether she'd have the same courage in Eduarda's place. Sometimes she was certain of one thing: Eduarda didn't see, didn't truly grasp, how brave she was being.
“And do you think she's okay?” Gerluce asked whenever they were together, every single day.

She'd seen Lorena once or twice, not much more than that. It was an agreement they'd reached together. Henrique, Violeta, and Gerluce, who weren't quite as close to Lorena or had been a little more distant, preferred to wait until she was moved into a regular room and well enough for longer, calmer visits. As a nurse, Gerluce knew some aspects of the ICU could be embarrassing, and none of them wanted Lorena to feel uncomfortable.
“I think she's progressing well, within expectations,” Eduarda began to explain.

For a moment she concentrated on traffic again, turning into a residential side street near her apartment. Gerluce, Paulo, Henrique, and Violeta were still camped out at her place. Eduarda couldn't decide whether she liked it or was being driven insane by so much movement and so many people in a space that had always been hers alone, but she had a feeling that wasn't going to change anytime soon. At least not while Lorena remained so fragile.
She stopped at another light behind the cars waiting ahead and continued.

“Her voice has improved a lot, she's pretty talkative now, but she still gets tired really fast. Eating is a disaster. It's hard to convince her to eat anything. It's complicated. She's still very weak, and she's aware of it now. This stage is awful, not being able to get out of bed, needing help with everything. I'm starting to get a little worried, honestly. I'm afraid Lorena might be getting depressed after so much time in the hospital, and...”

Eduarda stopped, glancing at the rearview mirror when the roar of a motorcycle interrupted her thoughts. The rider was doing what motorcyclists knew how to do best: ignoring every traffic law as he tried to squeeze between the tightly packed cars and run the red light. She was too tired to argue when she realized he was going to pass beside her.

“What the hell is this idiot doing? Can he seriously not see there's no room to get through here? He's going to rip off my side mirror and then I'll have to...” She broke off when, instead of continuing past, the motorcycle pulled up right beside her, just inches from the window.
The man riding it turned his helmet-hidden face toward her, and Eduarda had time for two things before she understood: to realize something was wrong, and to scream.
“Gerluce, get down!” She grabbed her friend by the arm without thinking and tried to curl in on herself, out of the line of fire, when she saw the barrel of a pistol aimed at her head.
Her eyes closed, and the last thing she heard was gunshots exploding in her ears.
